item.title: Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand
item.dc:creator: Stanislav Larinsky, Vladislav Vlasov, Boris Trefilov
item.description: We break down the Citrus Ransomware group's attacks: the attackers' TTPs and tooling, including VLESS traffic tunneling and LLM use, plus their links to Toy Ghouls.
item.content:encoded:
In recent years, cyberthreats have increasingly taken a hybrid approach, combining time-tested techniques for advancing through infrastructure, modern methods of evading network filters, and automation powered by large language models. This is also the approach of Citrus Ransomware, a previously undocumented group whose toolset includes VLESS tunnels (used to disguise traffic as regular HTTPS) and a ransomware Trojan from the Sn00py family. The attackers also integrate LLMs (large language models) into the process of infrastructure compromise.

In this article, we review the tactics and techniques the group used in recent incidents.

Initial Access: attacks through contractors

The attackers gain initial access to victims’ infrastructure through compromised contractors. They use credentials stolen from these contractors’ employees to connect to corporate VPNs or directly to internet-facing terminal servers over RDP.

Execution: commands, LLMs, and Impacket

The attackers run commands on compromised systems through the standard Windows command interpreter and PowerShell. As the attack progresses, they create and run PowerShell scripts, batch files, and commands generated by LLMs. One example of the latter is the commands below, which disable the account of one of the administrators.

Comment translation

# Disable account
# Verify result

Both commands come with comments, something attackers rarely bother with, so the comments very likely point to LLM use. And the models did more than generate commands. The attackers also produced full scripts, complete with the comments typical of LLM output.

Comment translation

# Creating background tasks for each computer with a thread limit
# Concurrent task limit control
# Quick ping

The fragment above comes from a script Citrus used to enumerate active user sessions on domain systems.

Besides LLMs, the attackers use atexec, a classic tool from the Impacket collection, to create scheduled tasks that run commands on hosts:

Task name Launched executable file
sIErKswD C:\Windows\System32\..\System32\cmd.exe
PpMBCCSR C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe
QwZtLmNp C:\Windows\..\Windows\System32\cmd.exe

We did not see the exact commands behind these tasks, but Group Policy was refreshed after they ran, so they most likely executed gpupdate /force.

When the group compromises 1C:Enterprise servers, it uses external data processors (1C-Shell) to run commands.

Persistence: scheduled tasks

Citrus uses scheduled tasks to launch its malicious tools automatically. The attackers create the tasks manually through PowerShell:

On systems that are not regularly rebooted, such as terminal servers, they sometimes run their tools without establishing persistence at all.

Privilege Escalation: vulnerabilities and configuration flaws

In every case we know of, the contractor domain account used for initial access had very limited privileges, so the attackers tried to escalate them.

To do this, they attempted to exploit the authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost); these attempts created machine accounts with telltale names in Active Directory, such as:

  • GHOSTAUFTAFGS
  • GHOSTCZYQVAZS
  • GHOSTIVPRLDZA
  • GHOST{8 random letters}

These names are generated by scripts making use of an exploit published on GitHub.

The exploit works like this: on behalf of the newly created account, it requests a certificate based on the Machine template from the system holding the AD CS role. The Attributes, Subject, and SubjectAlternativeName fields contain parameters like these:

<Data Name='Attributes'>CertificateTemplate:Machine\nSAN:dns=dc01.victim.domain\ncdc:91.210.109[.]118\nrmd:dc01.victim.domain
</Data>
<Data Name='Subject'>CN=GHOSTABUIEFAD.victim.domain</Data>
<Data Name='SubjectAlternativeName'>DNS name =dc01.victim.domain\r\n</Data>

The cdc attribute specifies the IP address or name of the system that the certification authority must contact to verify the data. The attackers specify the address of a system they control (in this case, 91.210.109[.]118) and send forged data from it. If exploitation succeeds, the certification authority issues a certificate with the specified parameters, based on the specified template.

Once the certificate is issued, the domain controller name in its SubjectAlternativeName field lets the attackers authenticate as the domain controller account.

In one case, the attackers also uploaded an executable for persistence, on behalf of which PowerShell scripts were launched with nonstandard HostName (Имя узла) field value.

Field name translation

Severity
HostName
HostVersion
HostId
HostApplication
EngineVersion
RunspaceId
PipelineId
CommandName
CommandType
ScriptName

Although the file was later deleted, indirect evidence hints at its purpose. For example, the MSFConsole value may indicate that the file is a component of the Metasploit framework. The PowerShell scripts run through this file included an exploit for the CVE-2020-1337 vulnerability; the same exploit is available in the Metasploit GitHub repository.

Beyond classic vulnerabilities in Microsoft products, the attackers also took an interest in 1C:Enterprise servers with insecure configurations (article in Russian).

On top of the configuration flaws, 1C:Enterprise systems are frequently accessed by support staff and administrators who hold elevated privileges in Active Directory. Together, these factors make it easy for attackers to escalate privileges and start moving laterally.

Stealth: covering tracks and masquerading

To hinder incident response, the attackers delete their tools and output files and clear the command history.

While the tools are still in use in the victim’s infrastructure, the attackers typically give them and their auxiliary objects legitimate-looking names:

  • KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64.exe and KasperskyGPO_Deploy_64_FIXED.exe are self-extracting archives. They contain the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script, a directory with a malicious Group Policy Object, and one of two archives, KasperskyAgent.exe or agent.exe.
  • KasperskyAgentInstaller.exe, KasperskyAgent.exe, and agent.exe are self-extracting archives containing the ransomware Trojan executable and auxiliary files.
  • Kaspersky GPO is the name of the Group Policy Object that distributes the ransomware Trojan in the victim’s infrastructure.
  • KasperskyAgentInstallTask and Sysvc are names used for the scheduled task that runs the self-extracting ransomware archive files.
  • Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 is the PowerShell script that creates the malicious Kaspersky GPO.
  • Kaspersky_GPO_Deployment.log is the log of the Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1 script.

Note that using the Kaspersky name in malicious file names doesn’t help the attackers avoid detection. Kaspersky solutions successfully detect and block these malicious files.

Defense Impairment: weak access policies for security tools play into attackers’ hands

To stay under the radar longer, the attackers clear event logs on some systems using the built-in wevtutil utility.

In addition, once they have sufficient privileges, they disable antivirus protection on hosts, which lets them run tools such as mimikatz.

The attackers also go after the centralized management consoles for security solutions, which they then use to disable protection en masse.

At the Impact stage, the attackers also use a Group Policy Object that modifies Windows Defender settings in the registry to switch it off. As a result, the antivirus did not respond when the ransomware was launched.

Finally, if they have sufficient privileges, the attackers manually add their malicious tools to the antivirus exclusion list.

Credential Access: mimikatz, a keylogger, and extraction of credentials from files

To capture keystrokes on a compromised system, the attackers use a modified version of the peeping-tom keylogger, whose source code is available on GitHub. The keylogger executable and its log file are located at the following paths:

  • C:\ProgramData\Oracle\Java\jhost.exe
  • C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\CLR\ErrorLog.txt

In the sample we found, stolen data was sent to 91.210.109[.]118. Persistence for the keylogger is provided by the scheduled task described above in the Persistence section.

To dump credentials from memory, the attackers use mimikatz. Files related to mimikatz are located at the following paths:

  • C:\ProgramData\x64\mimidrv.sys
  • C:\ProgramData\x64\mimikatz.exe
  • C:\ProgramData\x64\mimilib.dll
  • C:\ProgramData\x64\mimispool.dll

To hunt for credentials and other secrets (SSH keys, access tokens, and the like) in files on accessible network shares, the group uses Snaffler. To simplify running the tool, the attackers drop a configuration file on the system:

Besides data from network shares, the attackers were interested in data stored in password managers (for example, KeePass) on administrator workstations.

Discovery: the standard toolkit

Local discovery

After gaining control of a compromised system, the attackers ran a basic set of commands to identify the current user, running processes, network interface settings, the system’s external IP address, and so on:

whoami
tasklist
quser
ipconfig
curl 2ip[.]io

Remote discovery

In the early stages, the attackers used the fscan scanner to gather information on the internal infrastructure. They were particularly interested in the following ports:

  • 135 (RPC)
  • 139 (NetBIOS-SSN)
  • 1433 (Microsoft SQL)
  • 8006 (Proxmox VE)

Once they had the access they needed and had moved laterally, the attackers ran ADRecon on domain controllers and SharpHound on one of the workstations.

The attackers also used PowerShell to run LDAP queries against the controllers of adjacent domains, pulling lists of domain systems, users, and groups.

Russian text translation

The user has no additional groups in memberOf (primary only)
User not found

As an alternative to PowerShell, the attackers used the net.exe utility to get information about domain users and privileged groups:

net users /domain
net group "Domain Admins" /domain
net group "Администраторы домена" /domain

Lateral Movement: SSH, RDP, and WinRM

For lateral movement, the group relies on standard remote administration protocols: SSH, WinRM, and RDP. The attackers connect to systems either through previously deployed tunnels or directly from the compromised host.

Command and Control: delivering tools to the system

To deliver its tools to target hosts, the group uses built-in OS utilities. Specifically, the incidents involved:

  1. certutil:
  2. The Windows BITS background service (invoked in two ways):
  3. cURL:
  4. PowerShell:

Creating tunnels with Xray

The certutil and BITS commands shown above are what the attackers used to download Xray onto victim systems. They then used Xray to set up reverse VLESS tunnels to the command-and-control server. The configuration file, stored alongside the Xray executable, was usually named config.json. In some cases, the attackers deleted it right after starting the tunnel to hide the Xray configuration from defenders.

Judging by the configuration files recovered during the analysis, the attackers used port 443 on the VLESS server to blend in with legitimate HTTPS traffic. The configuration files also contain blocks that set up the REALITY protocol, which is intended to disguise the attackers’ traffic as requests to the legitimate site mirror.yandex.ru:

The traffic was also disguised as requests to another legitimate site, yastatic.net:

Installing AnyDesk

The PowerShell command above AnyDesk, which the attackers used to remotely control compromised hosts.

After the download, the attackers installed the software with the --silent flag to avoid alerting the user, set a connection password, and used PowerShell to pull the infected machine’s ID (which AnyDesk uses for remote connections on the client side) from the configuration file:

Collection & Exfiltration: data from messaging apps

Right before encrypting the data, the attackers connected to one of the domain controllers and ran the PowerShell script steal_tgs.ps1, which created the tdatas directory. According to the NTFS USN journal, while the script ran, 7-Zip created archives in this directory with telltale names hinting at their contents:

<system_name>_<date>_<username>_tdata.zip

The directory name tdatas and the substring tdata may refer to the C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\Telegram Desktop\tdata directory. The Telegram messaging app uses this directory to store authorization keys, session data, app settings, and other session information.

So the attackers were harvesting messaging app data from remote systems they could reach, packing it with 7-Zip and uploading it to an external web service through Google Chrome.

Impact: Sn00py ransomware Trojan

The Citrus group uses ransomware from the Sn00py family to encrypt data. It’s written in Go and uses the RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 algorithms to encrypt user files (but not system files) on Windows systems. Encrypted files receive the .citrus extension. For now, decryption is impossible without the attackers’ private key.

When launched, the ransomware opens a console on the victim’s device, where it outputs the commands it runs. It also attempts to modify the boot configuration data (BCD) by invoking a nonexistent executable, bcedit (likely a typo for bcdedit):

The ransomware’s console output contains the string:

We`re going to do something special today :). Made with RaaS platform Sn00py.

The string likely means the ransomware is distributed under the ransomware-as-a-service model, where attackers don’t write the malware themselves but subscribe to a ready-made offering.

The ransomware configuration contains the Citrus group’s public key in the pubkey parameter:

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
A7+eV3M+EDIh5kId+vf46QkKpAOKxUxv97PDFj66ox+uE0GV9UQhrSmBAoGAcyNI
+z7noIwrFYnHi6wtj8gLEOT0hE/cNDp0VLoUnAzi551kZA7J3Q575jwqrJcDrZSO
JLkZX7pxLLSd9iQdxMxDrLYZGRtiht8ToD5OGZri36oPvnW56ijJZ/NMzlFtVr7V
iSZJr5Qkz2cxShcSuhDLLXmzleclBd7HQtWTuZUCgYEAqN8WFAZxkV2e1p4v3U98
VOu4XxEfqAc2Gs2Ccs/kkWoX/1fxvuSRcF6/hMdfVwUP0z+/fnhbFMNfysBeWo1W
ZfmpBF/HbnRSg2ZDLWIwXEXEsNNSRmlvwyHWSEZgyG1xjgjSZKWuxo92WVmPxb5i
S6NLrZkHPHwqaBy8CnD6ft8=
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----

The host_blacklist parameter also lists the system names that are exempt from encryption:

[
    "DC01",
    "DC02",
    "DC03",
    "DC04"
]

This list includes the domain controllers used to distribute the policy that launches the ransomware. This way, the attackers ensure the policy keeps propagating uninterrupted.

As it runs, the Trojan drops CITRUS_README.txt files containing the ransom note:

-[ All your data were encrypted ]
|
|-If you try to decrypt them yourself, you will lose your data. To decrypt all systems, you need to contact us for guidance and a data recovery tool in the future. If you ignore our offer and the conversation does not take place, we will take extreme measures against your company and your employees, as a result of which you will lose access to all resources of your network and lose your reputation.
|
|-To contact us - register your mail here: https://account.proton.me/mail/signup?plan=free and write to us by email: [REDACTED]
|-Further negotiations regarding this situation will be conducted there. Also we have Telegram: [REDACTED]
|
|-Be sure to use a VPN, and do not attempt to write from other email addresses, as there is a high chance that the messages will not be delivered to either party.
|
|-You have 72 hours to contact us to establish negotiations and interaction, starting from the date of creation of this file.
|-If you do not contact us within 3 days, we will consider this a refusal to cooperate. This will entail immediate measures, such as: Dumps of your services, personal data of employees, accounting, contracts and source code.
|
|-Warning:
\\_ Do not delete, modify, or attempt to recover files by any means other than using our key and decryptor. This will damage your data, and we cannot guarantee its recovery.
\\_ Do not try to make this public, as you will only harm yourself and your reputation.

As mentioned above, the group uses malicious Group Policy Objects to launch the ransomware across victim systems en masse. The GPOs are created by self-extracting archives, of which we have seen two versions. Each archive contains:

  • A self-extracting archive with the ransomware Trojan and auxiliary files.
  • A directory containing the Group Policy Object. The policy drops the ransomware archive on the target system, creates a scheduled task that runs the archive with the parameters /quiet /norestart, enables the WinRM service, and disables the Volume Shadow Copy service and Windows Defender antivirus protection. It also sets a desktop wallpaper displaying the ransom note.
  • A PowerShell script that copies the ransomware archive to the \\<current_domain_name>\SYSVOL directory on the domain controller and links the malicious GPO to the domain using the Import-GPO and New-GPLink

One version of the PowerShell script contained comments suggesting that it was likely edited with an LLM:

Links to Toy Ghouls

While analyzing Citrus activity, we noticed several similarities to Toy Ghouls. Although their infrastructures don’t directly overlap, the two groups share TTPs: they encrypt their victims’ systems, use a similar set of tools (1C-Shell for remote command execution on 1C:Enterprise servers, mimikatz, PsExec, and ADRecon), and store these tools in the same directories. What’s more, both groups are Russian-speaking and attack Russian companies only. In several incidents, we saw the same infrastructure compromised simultaneously by both Toy Ghouls and Citrus.

Conclusion

What makes Citrus interesting is its unconventional approach to network tunneling and its use of AI to generate auxiliary tools. Even so, the attackers largely rely on well-known tools and techniques, which makes early detection somewhat easier. Kaspersky solutions detect all the activity described in this article.

That said, the Citrus attacks are another reminder that contractor access to an organization’s infrastructure must be tightly controlled and restricted. After all, compromising contractor accounts is exactly how the attackers get into their victims’ networks. We’ll continue to track the group’s activity and report new techniques as we discover them.

item.title: IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics
item.dc:creator: AMR
item.description: Key trends and statistics on malware targeting Windows and macOS computers and Internet of Things (IoT) devices in Q3 2026.
item.content:encoded:
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The statistics in this report are based on detection verdicts returned by Kaspersky products unless otherwise stated. The information was provided by Kaspersky users who consented to sharing statistical data.

Quarterly figures

In Q3 2026:

  • Kaspersky products blocked more than 311 million attacks launched from online resources.
  • Web Anti-Virus responded to 47 million unique links.
  • File Anti-Virus blocked more than 23 million malicious and potentially unwanted objects.
  • There were 4470 new ransomware variants discovered.
  • More than 81,000 users experienced ransomware attacks.
  • 15% of all ransomware victims whose data was published on threat actors’ data leak sites (DLSs) were victims of Qilin.
  • More than 217,000 users were targeted by miners.

Ransomware

Quarterly trends and highlights

Threat actor disruption

In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments.

In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims.

Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit.

Vulnerabilities and attacks

In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts.

CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups:

  • CVE-2026-15409/CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom.
  • CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution.
  • CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally.
  • CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.
  • CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution.
  • CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity allowed OS commands to run with the privileges of the TeamCity server process by way of an authentication bypass through the agent polling protocol. Command execution at that level could give access to configurations, credentials, CI/CD pipelines, and more.

The most prolific groups

This section highlights the most prolific ransomware gangs by number of victims added to each group’s DLS. Qilin (15.39%) holds first place, as it did last quarter. Qilin is followed by The Gentlemen (7.89%), which was especially active in Q1 but did not make the list in Q2. A notable newcomer on the list is Deadlock (4.46%), a relatively young ransomware family first reported in July 2025.

Number of each group’s victims according to its DLS as a percentage of all groups’ victims published on all the DLSs under review during the reporting period (download)

Number of new ransomware variants

In Q3, Kaspersky products detected three new ransomware families and 4470 new variants, more than 1.5 times last quarter’s count.

Number of new ransomware modifications, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

Number of users attacked by ransomware Trojans

During the reporting period, our products protected 81,556 unique users from ransomware attacks. Users encountered ransomware most often in September.

Miners

Number of new miner variants

In Q3 2026, Kaspersky solutions detected 2197 new miner variants. After the spike in the second quarter, it’s fair to say the pattern has returned to the calmer one typical of last year.

Number of new miner modifications, Q3 2026 (download)

 

Number of users attacked by miners

In Q3, we detected miner attacks on the computers of 217,024 unique Kaspersky users worldwide.

Attacks on macOS

Quarterly highlights

At the beginning of the third quarter, Jamf researchers discovered a new stealer, PamStealer. What sets it apart is its use of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) to verify the administrator password the user enters.

During the quarter, Socket researchers discovered several supply chain attacks that compromised popular npm, PyPI and Cargo (the Rust package manager) packages. The malicious payloads in these packages targeted macOS systems along with others. For example, on July 11, an infected npm package, jscrambler, was published. Its malicious module was an infostealer written in Rust. The infostealer targeted crypto wallets, secrets from various services and browsers, MCP server configurations, and API keys for AI agents. In August, an attack was detected on the arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec Rust crates; it delivered a Rust backdoor to the victim’s device. In September, malicious versions of the MemTensor npm and PyPI packages were published. They delivered a Go backdoor that targeted secrets, configurations, and API tokens of various services.

In August, Jamf researchers also reported discovering a new backdoor, Overlord. It was distributed as fake Zoom installers and had fairly broad spyware functionality, which is not often seen in macOS backdoors: it could eavesdrop through the microphone, watch the user through the camera, capture the screen, and log keystrokes.

In the third quarter, we discovered an updated version of the MacSync crypto stealer and backdoor with a significantly changed payload delivery method.

TOP 20 threats to macOS

Unique users who encountered this malware as a percentage* of all attacked users of Kaspersky security solutions for macOS (download)

* Data for the previous quarter may differ slightly from previously published data due to certain verdicts being retrospectively revised.

The share of Ngrok, a network tunneling tool suite with both legitimate and malicious uses, continued to grow, bringing it to the top of the list. We’re also seeing more detections of the well-known Amos malware, both the traditional stealer and a version with backdoor functionality.

This section presents statistics on attacks targeting Kaspersky IoT honeypots. The geographic data on attack sources is based on the IP addresses of attacking devices.

Attacks via web resources

The statistics in this section are based on detection verdicts by Web Anti-Virus, which protects users when suspicious objects are downloaded from malicious or infected web pages. These malicious pages are purposefully created by cybercriminals. Websites that host user-generated content, such as message boards, as well as compromised legitimate sites, can become infected.

TOP 10 countries and territories that served as sources of web-based attacks

The following statistics show the distribution by country/territory of the sources of internet attacks blocked by Kaspersky products on user computers (web pages redirecting to exploits, sites containing exploits and other malware, botnet C&C centers, and so on). One or more web-based attacks could originate from each unique host.

To determine the geographic source of web attacks, we matched each domain name to the actual IP address hosting it, then geolocated that address (GeoIP).

In Q3 2026, Kaspersky solutions blocked 311,083,655 attacks launched from online resources across the globe. Web Anti-Virus was triggered by 46,936,926 unique URLs.

Statistics on local infections of user computers are an important indicator. item.title: IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics
item.dc:creator: Anton Kivva
item.description: Q3 2026 mobile threat statistics for Android malware, adware, and unwanted software, plus the most notable malware found during the quarter.
item.content:encoded:
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

The mobile section of the quarterly cyberthreat report includes statistics on malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software for Android, as well as descriptions of the most notable threats for Android and iOS discovered during the reporting period. These statistics are based on detection alerts from Kaspersky products, collected from users who consented to provide statistical data to Kaspersky Security Network.

The quarter in figures

According to Kaspersky Security Network, in Q3 2026:

  • More than 1.66 million attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software were blocked.
  • The Trojan-Banker category was the prevalent mobile malware threat with a 31.63% share of all detected malicious apps.
  • Over 378,000 malicious installation packages were detected, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages.

Quarterly highlights

In July, we discovered a malicious app targeting Brazilian users that may have used AI to automate fraud. The app was disguised as Google Play Protect, a suite of security services for Android devices.

Malicious app imitating Google Play Protect

The app’s code used the DistilBERT model to interpret natural-language commands sent from the C2 server. Traces left in the code suggest the server-side commands may also have been generated by a large language model (LLM).

In August, we discovered a Trojan that analyzed images saved in the device’s gallery and took screenshots to look for banking data, including CVV codes. The malware used an on-device AI model to classify images. The app could also update this model, which gave the scammers a way to expand the Trojan’s functionality.

In the third quarter, the infamous subscription Trojan detected as Trojan.AndroidOS.Subscriber.bh made it into Google Play again. This time, it was disguised as an app for creating keyboard themes.

Subscription Trojan disguised as a keyboard theme app

The Trojan opened a subscription link in a hidden WebView and intercepted the message containing the confirmation code. According to our data, the scammers mainly targeted users in Thailand.

There were also new attacks on iOS users. In August, researchers at Socket discovered 13 infected PHP packages in the Packagist repository. The malicious payload injected links to fraudulent casinos into sites that used these packages and, on iOS devices only, a hidden iframe that loaded the DarkSword exploit kit. The attack delivered a spyware module that stole keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and other personal data. Other modules found in this campaign were used to steal crypto wallet data and the seed phrases used to recover them.

SlowMist researchers found the same DarkSword exploit chain used in a fake app, FomoPeek. FomoPeek was published in the App Store, presenting itself as a crypto wallet tracker. The malware was designed to steal data from notes and crypto wallet apps.

Also in August, we discovered infected versions of popular iOS apps distributed through Telegram (link in Russian). To install such an app, the attackers asked users to buy a developer certificate. The modified versions contained a malicious module that collected device information, took screenshots, and sent this data to a server.

Mobile threat statistics

The downward trend in attacks on mobile devices involving malware, adware, or unwanted software continued: the number fell to 1,668,368 in Q3 from 1,996,823 in Q2.

Attacks on users of Kaspersky mobile solutions, Q1 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

In the third quarter, this decline was driven in part by fewer adware attacks, which we examine in more detail below.

The number of Android malware samples grew compared to the previous reporting period, reaching 378,456.

Detected malicious and potentially unwanted installation packages, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

The distribution of detected installation packages by type was as follows:

Detected mobile apps by type, Q2*–Q3 2026 (download)

* Data for the previous quarter may differ slightly from previously published data due to certain verdicts being retrospectively revised.

The sharp rise in Trojan-Dropper apps comes from more droppers delivering known banking Trojans such as Mamont and Creduz. In the previous quarter, we described the trend of attackers “packaging” banking Trojans. The resulting malware is classified as droppers, which explains the growth. Note that standalone banking Trojans still rank first. Together with droppers, they account for more than half of all detected malicious apps.

Share* of users attacked by the given type of malicious or potentially unwanted apps out of all targeted users of Kaspersky mobile products, Q2–Q3 2026 (download)

* The total percentage may exceed 100% if the same users encountered multiple attack types.

The number of AdWare.AndroidOS.HiddenAd and AdWare.AndroidOS.MobiDash attacks continued to decline, although adware traditionally ranks first by the number of attacked users. The growing share of Trojan-Dropper correlates with the increase in packaged banking Trojans described in the previous section. Among Trojan-Spy attacks, the biggest growth came from the BTMOB and SpyNote RAT Trojans, which are used to steal money.

Most of the list is made up of variants of Trojans that were already popular last quarter: several versions of the preinstalled Triada Trojan, Mamont bankers, and BTMOB spyware.

The main newcomer among Q3’s most widespread malware was the Trojan-Proxy.AndroidOS.Vo1d.b apps, delivered by preinstalled Trojans. These apps turn the device into an exit node of a VPN service. These attacks are dangerous for two reasons. First, they burn through internet traffic, which the user may be paying for, to relay other people’s data. Second, cybercriminals can use the infected device to attack online services and visit banned websites, breaking the law in the victim’s name.

Mobile banking Trojans

In Q3 2026, the number of Trojan-Banker installation packages began rising again after a drop last quarter.

Number of installation packages for mobile banking Trojans detected by Kaspersky, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 (download)

By type, Creduz again accounts for the largest share of banking Trojans. However, as in Q2, the statistics of actual attacks tell a different story: Mamont variants were again the most active Trojans.
